question: A solid object is fully submerged in water and remains suspended at that depth, neither rising nor sinking. Which statement about the forces acting on the object is correct?
options: The buoyant force on the object is greater than its weight.
The buoyant force on the object equals its weight.
The buoyant force on the object is less than its weight.
The buoyant force on the object is zero while it is fully submerged.
gold_answer: The buoyant force on the object equals its weight.
notes: Question, options and claims are original wording. All evidence passages are verbatim excerpts from OpenStax, College Physics (1e), section 11.7 Archimedes' Principle, retrieved 2026-11-19; that book is released under the Creative Commons Attribution licence (CC BY 4.0). All nine claims draw on this single section; a second independent source is recommended before freezing.

positions.answer: The buoyant force on the object is greater than its weight.

claims.text: The buoyant force is the net upward force on any object in a fluid.

evidence.text: The buoyant force is the net upward force on any object in any fluid.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage defines the buoyant force as the net upward force on any object in any fluid, which entails the claim directly.

claims.text: An object remains suspended at a depth when the buoyant force on it is greater than its weight.

evidence.text: If the buoyant force is greater than the object's weight, the object will rise to the surface and float. If the buoyant force is less than the object's weight, the object will sink. If the buoyant force equals the object's weight, the object will remain suspended at that depth. The buoyant force is always present whether the object floats, sinks, or is suspended in a fluid.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage assigns suspension at depth to equality of buoyant force and weight, and assigns a buoyant force greater than the weight to rising and floating. Both statements refute the claim as written.

claims.text: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the object.

evidence.text: Stated in words, Archimedes' principle is as follows: The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.
evidence.notes: Section 11.7, subsection 'Buoyant Force', statement of Archimedes' principle; verbatim.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced, not the weight of the object itself; the claim substitutes a different quantity.

positions.answer: The buoyant force on the object is greater than its weight.

claims.text: The buoyant force on an object is the downward force exerted by the fluid on the object.

evidence.text: The buoyant force is the net upward force on any object in any fluid.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage specifies that the net force is upward, so assigning it a downward direction reverses the stated relation.

claims.text: An object floats when the buoyant force on it exceeds its weight.

evidence.text: If the buoyant force is greater than the object's weight, the object will rise to the surface and float.
evidence.notes: Section 11.7, opening paragraphs; verbatim first sentence of the wider passage.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that a buoyant force greater than the object's weight makes the object rise to the surface and float, which entails the claim.

claims.text: The object in the question is made of steel.

evidence.text: Drop a lump of clay in water. It will sink. Then mold the lump of clay into the shape of a boat, and it will float. Because of its shape, the boat displaces more water than the lump and experiences a greater buoyant force. The same is true of steel ships.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage discusses clay and steel ships as illustrations but never identifies the material of the object in the question, so it neither establishes nor refutes the claim.

positions.answer: The buoyant force on the object equals its weight.

claims.text: If the buoyant force on an object equals its weight, the object will remain suspended at that depth.

evidence.text: If the buoyant force equals the object's weight, the object will remain suspended at that depth.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states this exact equality-to-suspension relation, so it entails the claim directly.

claims.text: The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

evidence.text: Stated in words, Archimedes' principle is as follows: The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

claims.verdict_rationale: The cited sentence is the statement of Archimedes' principle and matches the claim word for word.

claims.text: The buoyant force is always present whether an object floats, sinks, or is suspended in a fluid.

evidence.text: The buoyant force is always present whether the object floats, sinks, or is suspended in a fluid.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states this directly, so the claim is entailed.
